**Direct answer:** No. WAL doesn't eliminate write contention. SQLite in WAL mode still allows only one writer at a time. What WAL adds is that readers and writers no longer block each other. It also makes commits cheaper, so each write holds the lock for a shorter time.

I used three of the eight retrievals. They were all official SQLite pages, which is enough to answer the question. I did not look for independent benchmarks, so I can't give measured throughput numbers.

**Claims and sources**

- WAL lets readers and a writer run at the same time. Neither blocks the other.
  - https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

- The SQLite docs hedge that "writers don't block readers" is only "mostly true". The page doesn't spell out the exceptions in the part I read. Checkpoint and recovery behavior is the likely area, but that is my inference.
  - https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

- WAL permits only one writer at a time, because there is one WAL file. Writers still contend with each other.
  - https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

- SQLite supports many simultaneous read transactions but only one write transaction.
  - https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html

- A second writer gets `SQLITE_BUSY`. This also happens when a read transaction tries to upgrade to a write while another connection has modified or is modifying the database. `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` can fail with `SQLITE_BUSY` if another write transaction is active. Starting with `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` avoids the upgrade failure; that advice is my inference from the definitions, not something the page recommends.
  - https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html

- In WAL mode, `EXCLUSIVE` and `IMMEDIATE` behave the same.
  - https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html

- Stock WAL doesn't give concurrent writers. The experimental `BEGIN CONCURRENT` branch does. It works in `wal` or `wal2` mode and uses optimistic page-level conflict detection. A conflict fails the commit with `SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT`, and commits are still serialized. This is a separate branch, not standard SQLite.
  - https://www.sqlite.org/src/doc/begin-concurrent/doc/begin_concurrent.md

- WAL is faster "in most scenarios". Each write goes to the log once instead of twice, writes are sequential, and there are fewer `fsync()` calls. That shortens how long the single write lock is held.
  - https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

- WAL has costs:
  - It may be about 1–2% slower for mostly-read workloads.
  - Read performance degrades as the WAL file grows.
  - An occasional commit that triggers a checkpoint is much slower.
  - https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

- Checkpoint starvation: if there is always at least one active reader, checkpoints can't complete and the WAL file grows without bound.
  - https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

- Large transactions: before 3.11.0 (2016), WAL was worse for transactions over about 100 MB. From 3.11.0 on, it handles large transactions as efficiently as rollback mode.
  - https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

- WAL requires all processes to be on the same host and does not work over network filesystems.
  - https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

**Not established by these sources**

- Real-world throughput gains under write-heavy load. The docs say "faster in most scenarios" but give no figures.
- Exact `SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT` behavior in plain WAL. The transaction page doesn't cover it, and the rescode page would.

Sources:
- [SQLite: Write-Ahead Logging](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html)
- [SQLite: Transaction](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html)
- [SQLite: BEGIN CONCURRENT](https://www.sqlite.org/src/doc/begin-concurrent/doc/begin_concurrent.md)
